Wales was due to receive some £375 million a year in EU structural funding, and the commitment made during the referendum campaign, repeated in successive manifestos, was that Wales would not lose a penny as a result of our departure from the European Union. Yet the allocations announced so far amount to a fraction of that sum, and the methodology used to distribute them bypasses the Welsh Government entirely. That is not a technical quibble; it is a fundamental question about devolution and about trust. For more than two decades, the Welsh Government, working with local authorities, universities, the third sector and business, built up genuine expertise in designing programmes that matched investment to local need—programmes for skills, for town centre regeneration, for supporting people furthest from the labour market. That partnership approach was praised by the European Commission itself as an exemplar. To sweep it aside and administer funds directly from Whitehall, with competitive bidding rounds that pit one deprived community against another, is to discard hard-won institutional knowledge and to weaken the devolution settlement by the back door. I say to the Minister in all sincerity: local authorities in Wales are not asking for special treatment. They are asking for what was promised—full replacement of the funding, multi-year certainty so that they can plan properly, and respect for the democratic institutions that the people of Wales have twice endorsed in referendums. If the Government are serious about levelling up, they should start by honouring that commitment in full, publishing a clear reconciliation of the old funding against the new, and sitting down with Welsh Ministers as equal partners rather than treating them as an afterthought. Our communities deserve nothing less, and I hope the Minister will respond to those points directly today.

Under the old investor-state dispute settlement mechanism, foreign corporations were given the extraordinary power to sue our government, before private tribunals, for decisions taken democratically in the public interest. Canada became one of the most sued countries in the developed world under chapter 11. We paid out hundreds of millions of dollars, and beyond the payouts themselves there was the chill: governments at every level hesitating to strengthen environmental protections, to safeguard water, to respect indigenous title, for fear of triggering yet another claim from a multinational with deep pockets and patient lawyers. That is not what trade is supposed to be about. Trade is supposed to be about the exchange of goods and services to the mutual benefit of working people on both sides of the border, not about handing corporations a parallel legal system that ordinary Canadians could never access. When a small business in my riding has a grievance, it goes to court like everyone else. When an indigenous community sees its rights infringed, it must fight for years through our domestic system. Why should a foreign investor enjoy a faster, friendlier, private track? So while I have real criticisms of parts of the new agreement, and I will come to them, I want to be clear that the removal of these provisions between Canada and the United States is a genuine victory, and it is a victory that came about because civil society, labour unions, environmental organizations and indigenous peoples spent decades making the case that this House is finally hearing. The lesson we should draw is that these agreements are not handed down from on high, immutable and untouchable. They are negotiated by governments, and governments respond to pressure. Our job now is to remain vigilant, to ensure that what was removed does not creep back in through side letters or future annexes, and to insist that every future agreement this country signs puts sovereignty, the environment and indigenous rights ahead of investor privilege.

But precisely because the stakes are so high, the measures we adopt must command public confidence, and that means they must be evidence-based, clearly explained and fairly applied. My concern is that the current approach fails those tests in several respects. First, the evidence underpinning the specific restrictions has not been published in full. The figures I have seen suggest that hospitality accounts for a small fraction of identified transmission, far behind households and other settings, yet it bears the heaviest burden of restriction. Second, the economic support does not match the scale of the sacrifice being demanded. Two thirds of wages is not enough for someone on the minimum wage with rent to pay, and the exclusion of company directors and the newly self-employed from meaningful support remains a glaring injustice ten months into this crisis. Third, we still do not have a functioning system of test, trace and isolate, which every scientific adviser agrees is the way out of the cycle of blanket restrictions. Contact tracing rates in the areas under the tightest measures remain woefully inadequate, and support for people asked to isolate is so thin that many simply cannot afford to comply. So I say to the Minister: I will support proportionate action to save lives, but the Government must publish the evidence, fix the support, and give the House a proper opportunity to scrutinise and vote on these measures before they are imposed, not days afterwards. That is how consent is maintained in a democracy, even—especially—in an emergency.

I would also ask what training will accompany these changes. Sanctions deal with behaviour after the fact; culture prevents it in the first place. If we are honest, this institution has tolerated conduct for decades that would not have survived a week in a well-run modern workplace, and changing that requires more than a disciplinary code—it requires leadership from the top, consistently applied, without fear or favour, regardless of party or seniority. Nellie McClung and the Famous Five fought to have women recognized as persons under the law, and they won. Women won the vote, won the right to sit in this chamber, and have gone on to serve at the highest levels of government. Those victories were real and we honour them. But if we are honest with ourselves, Mr. Speaker, the promise of full and equal citizenship remains unfinished business in this country. Women in Canada still earn substantially less than men for work of equal value. Indigenous women and girls go missing and are murdered at rates that should shame us all, and the calls for justice from the national inquiry remain largely unanswered, gathering dust while families grieve. Women fleeing violence are turned away from shelters every single night because there is no room. Affordable child care, which we know is the single most powerful lever for women's economic participation, took generations to move from promise to policy, and we must ensure it is delivered in every community, rural as well as urban. And in this very chamber, women members still face harassment and abuse, particularly online, at levels their male colleagues do not experience, driving some of the best among us out of public life altogether. So when we quote Nellie McClung, let us not do so as a comfortable tribute to a battle safely won. Let us hear her words as she intended them—as a demand, an impatient demand, for what is owed. Give us our due. That means equal pay legislation with teeth. It means implementing the inquiry's calls for justice. It means shelters and housing and child care funded as the essential infrastructure they are. The women of this country have the brains to think, the hands to work and the hearts to feel. What they require from this Parliament is not more praise. It is action.

The first is clarity of obligation. A code that is vague helps nobody: large operators will lawyer their way around ambiguity, while smaller organisations, without compliance departments, will either over-comply at real cost or give up trying to understand their duties at all. The second is proportionality. The obligations must scale sensibly with the size and risk profile of the service, or we will entrench the very incumbents the regime is supposed to discipline. The third is enforceability. There is no point writing elegant codes if the regulator lacks the resources, the technical capability and the will to enforce them against the largest actors, and I would welcome an assurance about the resourcing that will accompany commencement. And it would be no answer, when those consequences arrive, to say that we did not choose them, for we will have chosen every step that led to them. So what is to be done in the time that remains? First, this House must stop pretending that refusing every available option is itself a policy. It is not; it is an abdication. Second, the Government must level with the public about the trade-offs, because the promise that we can retain every benefit while shedding every obligation has poisoned this debate from the beginning. Third, we should be prepared to seek the time needed to reach an agreement rather than treat the date in the calendar as more sacred than the interests of the country. History does not repeat itself, but as the saying goes, it often rhymes. The sleepwalkers of 1914 had the excuse that they could not see the precipice. We can see it perfectly well. If we walk over it regardless, with our eyes open, the judgment of history will be the harsher for it.

I understand the intention behind the amendment, and I want to address it seriously, because the treatment of holding deposits is one of the areas where the risk of abuse is most real. Under the Bill as drafted, a landlord or agent may retain a holding deposit only in defined circumstances—where the tenant withdraws, fails a right to rent check, or provides false or misleading information that materially affects their suitability. The question the hon. Member rightly poses is: how does the tenant know which of those grounds is being relied upon, and how can they challenge a retention they believe is unjustified? A tenant who has lost a week's rent, often at precisely the moment when they are trying to scrape together funds for another property, is poorly placed to pursue a dispute in the dark. Where I part company with the amendment is on the mechanism rather than the principle. Placing a freestanding statutory duty in the Bill, with its own enforcement provisions, would add complexity to a regime that we have deliberately tried to keep simple for tenants, landlords and enforcement authorities alike. What I can say is that the guidance to be issued alongside the Act will make clear that transparency about the reasons for retaining a holding deposit is expected as a matter of good practice, and that trading standards authorities will be able to take a pattern of unexplained retentions into account when considering enforcement action. I would add that the tenant retains the ability to challenge a wrongful retention through the deposit protection schemes and, ultimately, the courts. We will keep this under review, and if the evidence after commencement shows that holding deposits are being retained without proper justification on any scale, we will not hesitate to return to the issue and legislate further.

These are distinct groups, governed by distinct legal frameworks, and conflating them serves nobody except those who wish to sow confusion and, frankly, fear. Let me take a moment to set out the distinction plainly. A person who arrives at our border and claims asylum is exercising a right that exists in Canadian law and in the international conventions this country helped to write after the Second World War. They are not queue-jumpers, because there is no queue for asylum; the right to seek protection attaches to the person, wherever and however they arrive. Their claim is then tested—rigorously—before the Immigration and Refugee Board, with security screening from the moment of first contact. Some claims succeed; many do not, and those whose claims fail are subject to removal. That is the system working as designed. Separately, Canada runs one of the world's most admired resettlement programs, through which refugees identified overseas, often after years in camps, are brought here as permanent residents, many sponsored by church groups and community organizations in every one of our ridings. Both of these streams reflect who we are as a country, and both operate under the rule of law. When members stand in this place and blur those categories—when they describe asylum seekers as illegal, or imply that a person crossing between ports of entry has thereby forfeited due process—they are not merely making a legal error. They are corroding public confidence in a system that depends on public confidence to survive. There are legitimate debates to be had about resources, about processing times, which are far too long, and about the safe third country agreement itself. I welcome those debates. But let us conduct them on the basis of what the law actually says, and with some regard for the human beings whose lives sit behind every file number.

Nobody on this side is arguing that the convention rights are optional extras or foreign impositions; they were drafted in large part by British lawyers, building on centuries of our own legal tradition, and they codify protections—against arbitrary detention, against torture, for fair trial and family life—that any decent legal system would recognise as fundamental. The resistance to writing the principles into the Bill tells its own story. Assurances at the Dispatch Box are worth something in this place, but they are not justiciable, they do not bind successor Ministers, and they offer no comfort to the individual whose rights are engaged at the sharp end of these provisions—who will be dealing not with the Minister but with an official applying guidance we have never seen, under pressure to meet targets we can only guess at. The rule of law is not a decoration to be displayed when convenient and folded away when it obstructs a policy objective. It is the thing that distinguishes us from the regimes we criticise, and our credibility when we urge other states to honour their international commitments—on trade, on security, on human rights—rests entirely on our own willingness to honour ours. So I say to the Minister: accept the amendment, or explain to the House precisely which of these principles the Government find so burdensome that they cannot be stated in statute. If there is a good answer to that question, we have not heard it yet, and I suspect that is because none exists.

The temperature climbs to many hundreds of degrees in seconds, the battery vents toxic and flammable gases, and the fire that results burns with an intensity that conventional extinguishers struggle to touch. A cell can reignite hours after it appears to have been put out. Now, why does this matter to the House? Because these batteries are no longer confined to laptops and phones. The fire services have been sounding the alarm with increasing urgency: fires of this kind have risen sharply year on year, and they have killed people—in stairwells, in bedrooms, in properties where a charging bike sat between a sleeping family and their front door. And here is the crucial point: a disproportionate share of these fires involve not the reputable products sold by established manufacturers, but cheap conversion kits, aftermarket chargers and substandard batteries bought online, frequently from third-party sellers on marketplaces that accept no meaningful responsibility for the safety of what they list. A product that would never make it onto the shelf of a high street retailer can be delivered to your door tomorrow with a few clicks. That is the gap in our regulatory framework, and it is a gap this House can close. We need online marketplaces to bear real legal responsibility for the safety of goods sold through their platforms. We need proper standards for conversion kits and chargers, enforced at the border and in the market. And we need a sustained public information campaign on safe charging, because until the law catches up, awareness is the best protection families have. Lives have already been lost. We should not wait to lose more before acting.

my quarrel is with a system that has normalised waiting as a form of rationing. Let us speak plainly about what the waiting lists mean in the life of a child. A three-year-old who needs speech and language therapy and waits eighteen months for an assessment is not simply delayed; the window in which intervention works best is closing while the child's name sits in a queue. A family told their son needs an assessment of need within the statutory timeframe, who then discover that the timeframe is honoured in the breach in almost every CHO area, learn quickly that the law as written and the service as delivered are two different countries. Parents in my constituency have described it to me as a full-time job—chasing referrals, photocopying reports, appealing decisions, being passed from primary care to disability services and back again, each service insisting the child belongs to the other. And those are the parents with the time, the English, the confidence and the resources to fight. The children of parents without those advantages simply disappear into the lists. That is the failure I am naming: not a failure of individual clinicians, who are as frustrated as the families, but a failure of workforce planning that has left therapist posts unfilled by the hundred, a failure of structure that fragments responsibility until no one holds it, and a failure of honesty in setting statutory entitlements that the State has no realistic plan to meet. So what I am asking of the Minister of State tonight is specific. First, publish the current vacancy figures for the children's disability network teams, area by area, so we can see the true scale of the gap. Second, set out the recruitment and training pipeline that will fill those posts, with numbers and dates rather than aspirations. Third, in the meantime, fund the interim supports—home tuition grants, private assessments where the public system cannot deliver—so that no child's development is sacrificed to an administrative failure. These children cannot wait, because childhood does not wait.

When I ask Ministers for detail, I am referred to the Joint Committee; when the Joint Committee is asked, we are told discussions are ongoing and confidential. Somewhere in that circle of deferral, the interests of actual traders have gone missing. So let me put three requests to the Minister, none of which, I believe, would prejudice any negotiation. First, publish a schedule of the Joint Committee's agenda items and expected decision points, so that Parliament and business alike can see what is being decided and when. Second, commit to a written ministerial statement after each meeting, setting out at minimum the matters discussed and any decisions reached—other international bodies manage this level of openness without the sky falling. Third, give an undertaking that no decision of the Joint Committee with significant implications for trade or for Northern Ireland will be implemented without a statement to this House and an opportunity for scrutiny. Trust in these arrangements, on all sides of the water and on all sides of this House, is fragile. Secrecy does not protect that trust; it corrodes it. Openness is not a concession to opponents of the agreement—it is the best defence its supporters have.

I want to be honest with the House about the stakes for Ireland. We are the member state most exposed to the consequences of these negotiations failing. A no-deal outcome would mean tariffs on our agri-food exports to Britain, our largest market for beef and cheddar, at rates that would make much of that trade simply unviable. It would mean disruption at ports for which no amount of preparation can fully compensate, and pressure on the all-island economy at exactly the moment when the protocol arrangements are bedding down. That is why the Government's approach has been consistent throughout: we support Michel Barnier and the Task Force fully, we do not negotiate bilaterally or seek side arrangements, and we work to ensure that Ireland's specific concerns—on the land bridge, on east-west trade, on the common travel area—are understood and reflected in the Union's position. And they are. I have spoken in recent days with President von der Leyen and with several of my counterparts, and I can tell the House that solidarity with Ireland remains rock solid, just as it was throughout the withdrawal negotiations. At the same time, we continue to intensify our domestic readiness: the Brexit omnibus legislation is before the Oireachtas, port and airport infrastructure has been expanded, and supports for the sectors most exposed are provided for in the budget. I remain of the view that a deal is possible and in everybody's interest, but it takes two to make an agreement, and the space for one is narrowing. Either way, Ireland will be as prepared as any country can be, and our place at the heart of the European Union is not in question.

Businesses emerged from the pandemic carrying debt they would never have chosen in normal times—bounce back loans, deferred VAT, rent arrears accumulated during the moratorium—only to walk straight into an energy crisis, surging input costs and rising interest rates that made every one of those liabilities heavier. The figures tell the story: insolvencies are running at their highest levels for years, and the businesses failing now are disproportionately the small and medium-sized firms—the shops, hospitality venues and small manufacturers—that survived the pandemic itself only to be finished off by its aftermath. There is something particularly bitter about a business that made it through lockdown, that did everything asked of it, closing its doors in the recovery because the repayment schedule collided with an energy bill that trebled. So the question before the House is what a responsible Government should do now. I would suggest three things. First, flexibility on repayment: the pay-as-you-grow arrangements were a good start, but they need extending and widening, because a viable business paying down debt slowly is worth infinitely more to the Exchequer than an insolvent one paying nothing at all. Second, HMRC's approach to time-to-pay arrangements needs to reflect current conditions; I hear too often from firms that the flexibility shown in 2020 and 2021 has been replaced by a rigidity that tips struggling businesses over the edge. Third, we need honesty about the commercial rent arrears that remain unresolved, where the arbitration scheme has helped some but left many tenants and landlords in a stand-off that benefits neither. The State stepped in during the emergency, rightly and at great cost. It would be a false economy of the worst kind to let the recovery fail for want of patience now.

However, a plan is only as good as its funding, its timelines and its willingness to name the causes of the problem, and it is against those tests that we will judge what the Minister of State has outlined today. Let us be honest about what has happened to our town centres. The dereliction and vacancy that scar the main streets of towns across this State are not natural phenomena; they are the product of policy choices made over decades—the hollowing out of town-centre retail by unbalanced planning decisions, the failure to tackle land hoarding and speculation, the absence of any serious scheme to bring the thousands of vacant units above shops back into residential use, and local authorities so starved of funding and staff that enforcement of the derelict sites legislation is sporadic at best. Sinn Féin has published detailed proposals in this area, and I offer them to the Minister of State constructively. We would put real teeth into the vacant sites and derelict sites regimes, with registers that are accurate and levies that are actually collected—because the Minister knows that collection rates at present are derisory. We would introduce meaningful, easily accessed grants to convert over-the-shop vacancy into homes, cutting through the fire certification and planning barriers that make such conversions unviable for ordinary owners. And we would ensure that local authorities have dedicated town regeneration officers, because a fund that requires a small town's voluntary committee to compete with consultant-written applications from better-resourced areas will entrench inequality rather than remedy it. The prize here is enormous: homes for people in the hearts of our towns, footfall for struggling businesses, and the revival of communities that have watched their main streets decline for a generation. We will support every genuine step in that direction, but we will also hold the Government to delivery, because our towns have had enough glossy strategies. What they need now is action.

Our allies have learned a painful lesson about what it means to depend on hostile powers for the fuel that heats their homes, and they have come to us asking whether Canada can help. It would be a failure of both economic sense and moral imagination to shrug and say we cannot. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I want to be clear that this is not an argument against the energy transition; it is an argument about how we get there. The transition will take decades, and during those decades the world will continue to consume oil and gas. The only question is who supplies it and under what standards. Meanwhile, the same resource base, the same skilled workforce and the same infrastructure corridors that serve our conventional industry are exactly what we need to build the industries of the future—hydrogen, critical minerals, nuclear, carbon capture. The workers in our energy sector are not the obstacle to a cleaner future; they are the people who will build it. Behind the statistics are the same recurring causes we have known about for years: speed, impairment, distraction by mobile phones, and roads—particularly rural roads—engineered for a different era. The response cannot be another round of appeals to personal responsibility alone. It must include enforcement, and here I have to put hard questions to the Minister. Garda roads policing numbers have fallen substantially from their peak. What use are penalties on the statute book if the realistic chance of detection keeps falling? The graduated driver licensing system remains incompletely enforced. Safety camera coverage, which the evidence shows saves lives wherever it is deployed, lags behind what the road safety strategy itself commits to. mourning. The attack on the Chabad house was not a random act of violence; it was an attack aimed deliberately at Jews, at a place of prayer, study and hospitality, a place whose doors are open to any Jewish traveller anywhere in the world, and often to anyone at all in need of a meal or a moment of refuge. That openness is the essence of what Chabad does, and it is precisely that openness that makes such places vulnerable to those who hate. Mr. Speaker, I rise today first to mourn with the families of the victims, with the Chabad movement, and with Jewish communities in Canada and around the world who feel this loss as their own. The emissaries who staff these houses—young couples, very often, who leave everything familiar to serve in distant places for their entire lives—represent a remarkable ideal of service. To attack them is to attack the very idea of welcome. But mourning is not enough, and this House knows it. Antisemitism is rising in our own country, not somewhere else, not in history books—here. Statistics on hate crimes tell us that Jewish Canadians remain among the most targeted religious communities in the country, year after year. Synagogues in our cities require security guards. Jewish schools conduct lockdown drills. Students on our campuses report hiding visible signs of their identity. This is Canada in the present day, and it should be intolerable to every member of this House regardless of party. So let us respond with more than words. Let us ensure that the security infrastructure program for communities at risk is funded to meet demand, not merely announced. Let us give law enforcement the direction and the tools to treat hate crimes with the seriousness they deserve. And let each of us, in our ridings, stand visibly with our Jewish neighbours—at their synagogues, at their community centres, at their Chabad houses—so they know they do not stand alone.

practices are simply incompatible with any serious understanding of animal welfare, and confining wild animals such as mink in small wire cages for the entirety of their lives, before killing them for a product nobody needs, is chief among them. Mink are semi-aquatic, solitary, wide-ranging animals. In the wild they swim, dive, hunt and patrol territories that can extend for miles of riverbank. In a fur farm they live in a cage measuring less than a square metre, in rows of thousands, with stereotypical behaviours—the endless pacing and self-mutilation that are the unmistakable signs of psychological distress—documented wherever investigators have looked. No enrichment measure, no code of practice, can reconcile the nature of the animal with the nature of the cage. That is why country after country across Europe has legislated for prohibition, and it is why the veterinary and scientific evidence presented to the Department has pointed so consistently in one direction. The pandemic added a further and frankly alarming dimension: we saw in Denmark and the Netherlands that mink are highly susceptible to coronavirus infection, that farms became reservoirs of the virus, and that mutations arose in farmed mink and passed back to humans, prompting the culling of millions of animals. A practice that was already ethically indefensible was revealed to be a public health liability as well. I acknowledge that for the small number of farms operating in the State, this legislation ends a legal livelihood, and the Bill is right to provide for fair compensation and support for the workers affected; that is how a State should behave when it changes the rules on people who operated within them. But the direction is clear and correct. This Bill does not merely close an industry; it states a principle—that in this Republic, the suffering of sentient creatures cannot be justified by fashion. I commend the Bill to the House and urge its swift passage.

our own waters. Some 15%—in the waters of which we are the coastal state, waters that our fleet has fished for generations, while vessels from other member states take the great bulk of what swims off our coast. And under the deal done on Brexit, it was Irish fishermen who were handed a wildly disproportionate share of the burden of quota transfers to Britain—a quarter of the entire EU transfer taken from the smallest fleets in the Union. Today, boats are tied up at the pier in Castletownbere, in Killybegs, in Howth, not because there are no fish but because their owners have no quota to catch them, while they watch factory vessels from other flags working the same grounds within sight of our shore. That is what is happening around our coast, and no amount of soft language about burden-sharing can disguise the raw unfairness of it. The tie-up schemes and decommissioning schemes that have been offered are not a policy; they are a managed retreat. We are paying our own fishermen to scrap their boats and leave the industry, in coastal communities where fishing is not just a job but the reason the community exists at all. When a trawler is decommissioned, it is not only a vessel that goes; it is the crew, the fuel supplier, the net maker, the processor, the young person who might have made a life at home instead of emigrating. So what am I asking of the Government? First, fight for burden-sharing at European level with the intensity this injustice deserves—the quota transfer must be rebalanced across the Union at the earliest review. Second, pursue every avenue for quota top-ups in our own zone. Third, invest in the inshore fleet and in processing so that more of the value of what is landed stays in our coastal communities. Our fishermen are not asking for special treatment. They are asking for a fair share of their own sea, and this State should not settle for anything less.

Write the secular ethos into its governing documents in terms that require no interpretation, no goodwill and no trust in assurances from any private body, religious or otherwise. The women of this country have a long and painful history with the entanglement of church and State in healthcare—in the Magdalen laundries, in the mother and baby homes, in symphysiotomy, in the denial of reproductive healthcare within living memory. That history is precisely why "trust us" is not an acceptable answer. It is why every ambiguity in these arrangements, every clause about "clinically appropriate" services, every layered structure of companies and designated activities, lands on ears that have heard careful reassurances before and learned what they were worth. A national maternity hospital, built with hundreds of millions of euro of public money, should be publicly owned, on publicly owned land, with an explicitly secular ethos guaranteeing that every service lawful in this State—every service—will be provided without exception, qualification or conscientious obstruction by the institution. That is not a radical demand; it is the bare minimum that public investment and public trust require. Until those conditions are met, the Minister should not proceed to cabinet with this proposal, and if he does, he should not be surprised that the women of Ireland, and this House, decline to take it on faith.

Second, on energy: every day, European payments for oil and gas fund the shells falling on Ukrainian cities. I recognise the difficulty for our European friends, but dependence that cannot be ended overnight can be ended deliberately, on a published timetable, and we should lead that effort rather than follow it. Third, on defence: the supply of weapons to Ukraine must be sustained and expanded, because the sanctions will take months to bite and the Ukrainians are fighting now. Fourth, we should be under no illusion about the information war; the Kremlin's propaganda networks should have no licence to broadcast in this country. And finally, we must be honest with our own constituents: doing this properly will carry costs at home—in energy prices, in inflation—and the Government must support households through them, because public consent for a long confrontation cannot be taken for granted. Putin's calculation is that our outrage will fade and our unity will fracture. The task of this House is to prove that calculation wrong, for as long as it takes.

Second, we must be careful that our aid continues to reach the people of Myanmar through civil society channels while ensuring not a dollar flows through the regime. Third, we should give every support to the efforts to ensure accountability—the evidence being gathered of crimes against humanity must one day meet justice, and the perpetrators should hear clearly that the world is keeping records. I want to explain to the House why this timeline, though later than anybody would wish, is the earliest achievable one. The written examinations require the full machinery of the State examinations system—the printing and secure distribution of papers, the appointment of superintendents and examiners, and above all the availability of school buildings and staff at a time when schools are also managing a full return under public health conditions. Running examinations for those students who choose to sit them, in parallel with the calculated grades process for the majority, is something the system has never previously attempted, and I will not risk the integrity of either process by rushing it. Let me also address the position of the students themselves, because they are at the centre of every decision here. Every student will receive their calculated grades in September, in time for CAO offers and college entry this year—no student is waiting on the November examinations to progress. The written examinations are there as an entitlement: any student who believes their calculated grade does not reflect their ability will have the opportunity to sit the paper, and they will be credited with whichever result is higher. Nobody can be worse off by sitting. That principle—no detriment—has guided the design throughout. I acknowledge the deputy's underlying point that this cohort of students has endured a level of disruption and anxiety that no previous Leaving Certificate class has faced, with schools closed for months and every certainty about their examinations shifting repeatedly through the spring. They have shown remarkable resilience. What they need from us now is stability: fixed dates published without delay, clear information through their schools, and supports in place for those preparing to sit papers in November. I am committed to delivering all three.

today put mine firmly in the shade. My story is a small one, but I think it says something true about her. Many years ago, long before I entered this House, I was present at an event that Her Majesty attended—one of hundreds she must have carried out that year, in a lifetime containing tens of thousands of them. I was a nobody in that room, standing at the end of a line, rehearsing what I might say if she came near and quietly hoping she would not. She did, of course. And what struck me then, and has stayed with me ever since, was not the ceremony of it but the opposite: she asked me a question, an ordinary question about who I was and what I did, and then she listened to the answer. She was not looking over my shoulder at the next person. For those thirty seconds, the most famous woman in the world gave every appearance of finding me interesting—and I have since learned that virtually everyone who met her tells a version of the same story. That, I think, was the secret hiding in plain sight. Duty, in her practice of it, was not the grand abstraction we make it in speeches; it was the accumulated weight of millions of small courtesies, performed identically for presidents and for nobodies, decade after decade, whether the cameras were present or not. Any of us can rise to a great occasion once. She treated every occasion as worth rising to, for seventy years, and she made each person in front of her feel that they were the occasion. In this place, we speak often of public service and mean, if we are honest, something that comes with recognition attached. Hers was the deeper kind: constancy without complaint, presence without ego. The finest tribute this House can pay her is not in our words this week but in whether any of that example rubs off on us. May she rest in peace.

improve ventilation in classrooms. Thirty months. Let that sink in: a child who was in year 7 when the Government first acknowledged that ventilation mattered will be sitting GCSE options before the evidence from a single pilot study is fully before us—and that is before a decision is taken, before procurement, before a single additional purifier arrives in a classroom as a result. This is not how a Government behaves when it regards a problem as urgent. Compare the timeline with what we already know. The science on airborne transmission has been settled for years. The Health and Safety Executive and SAGE said repeatedly that ventilation is a critical control. Other countries did not wait: Germany allocated hundreds of millions of euros for air filtration in schools and public buildings; parts of the United States funded classroom HEPA filtration at scale through their recovery programmes. The technology in question is not experimental—HEPA filtration is used in hospitals and laboratories precisely because it demonstrably removes airborne particles, including virus-carrying aerosols. What the Bradford study can add is useful operational detail about deployment in classrooms; what it cannot justify is treating the basic question as open for two and a half years while children sit in rooms where the CO2 monitors the Government did supply are regularly reading levels that indicate poor ventilation with no means of acting on the information. And this is not only about covid. Clean air in classrooms reduces the transmission of flu and other winter viruses that drive absence among pupils and staff every single year; it improves concentration; and for the thousands of children with asthma it is a daily health issue. The investment required is modest by the standards of what this House routinely approves. So my question to the Minister is direct: will the Government stop hiding behind a pilot study and commit now to a funded programme of air cleaning in schools, prioritising the classrooms the CO2 data has already identified?

That is the central economic as well as moral point: early intervention for single homeless people is cheap; rough sleeping is extraordinarily expensive, in health services, in the justice system, in lost lives. Our Committee's recommendations follow from that logic. The prevention duty needs to be real, with housing authorities held to the quality of the help they give, not merely the fact of having given some. The local housing allowance must bear some relation to actual rents, because no amount of advice conjures up a tenancy that arithmetic makes impossible. And we need a proper supply of one-bedroom social homes and supported housing, the tenure types we have built least of for decades. I hope that when the Minister responds, we hear not a defence of the current framework but a recognition that, for single people, it is failing—and a plan to fix it.

They are tired of watching this place consume itself in procedural warfare while their real concerns—the cost of their weekly shop, the wait for a hospital appointment, the state of their local roads, the future of their children's jobs—go unaddressed month after month. Whatever side of the great divide of our politics they stand on, and my constituency contains multitudes on both, they share a growing conviction that Westminster has become a machine for generating heat without light. And here is what I find striking: when I hold surgeries or knock on doors, people who voted in opposite directions in the referendum can sit at the same kitchen table and agree within minutes on what actually needs doing—more GPs, decent buses, affordable homes for their kids, a high street that is not half-shuttered. The division that dominates this Chamber is real, but it is not the whole of the country, and we flatter ourselves if we think our obsessions are theirs. So I want to use my time to make a plea for proportion. By all means let us resolve the great constitutional question before us—we must, and I will set out my own view in a moment—but let us stop allowing it to be the excuse for the paralysis of everything else. Legislation on social care has been promised and postponed. The employment Bill has vanished. Towns like mine were promised transformation and have received consultations. I would caution against the assumption that sanctions alone constitute a strategy. The measures adopted have imposed real costs on the Russian economy—the evidence on capital flight, on borrowing costs and on foreign investment is clear—but the objectives for which they were imposed have not yet been achieved, and honesty requires us to acknowledge that. Sanctions are an instrument; they work best when they are part of a wider approach combining deterrence, diplomatic pressure and support for those on the receiving end of Russian aggression, and when they are maintained with patience and unity over time. That unity is the crucial point, and it is where my hon. Friend's question really bites. The European Union's sanctions require unanimity to renew, and we have all watched the Kremlin work assiduously on individual member states—through energy dependence, through financing of sympathetic political movements, through disinformation—precisely in order to fracture that consensus. So far, it has held, and that is an underappreciated diplomatic achievement, but it cannot be taken for granted, and Britain has played and must continue to play a leading role in stiffening it. Beyond sanctions, we press Russia in the other forums available to us: we have led in the OSCE and at the United Nations in calling out specific conduct; we have expelled intelligence officers operating under diplomatic cover, and persuaded an unprecedented coalition of allies to do likewise; and we continue to support the resilience of the states most exposed to Russian pressure, in the western Balkans and the eastern neighbourhood, because the contest is as much about their institutions as their borders. What we do not do—and I want to be clear about this—is confuse dialogue with weakness or isolation with strength. We keep channels open, as we must between nuclear powers, while being entirely realistic about the nature of the Russian state under its current leadership. It is a long game, my hon. Friend is right, and we intend to stay in it.

Research has shown for years that veterinary surgeons face a risk of suicide several times that of the general population—higher even than in the human medical professions. And here is why it matters beyond the profession itself: no vets, no food safety certification; no vets, no disease surveillance at the border; no vets, no animal welfare enforcement, no farm assurance, no pet care in rural communities. The veterinary workforce is national infrastructure, as surely as roads or broadband. On Holocaust Memorial Day, we remember the six million Jewish men, women and children murdered in the Shoah—a crime industrial in its organisation and intimate in its cruelty, carried out in the heart of educated, cultured Europe, within the lifetimes of people still among us. We remember, too, the other victims of Nazi persecution—Roma and Sinti people, disabled people, gay men, political prisoners—and the victims of the genocides that followed, in Cambodia, in Rwanda, in Bosnia, in Darfur, because the promise of "never again" has been broken too many times for us to treat remembrance as a comfortable ritual. This year, the act of remembrance carries a particular urgency, for two reasons. The first is that the generation of survivors is leaving us. The men and women who bore witness in our schools and community halls, who showed their tattoos to teenagers and answered their questions with patience and without bitterness, are now very few. The duty of memory is passing from those who saw to those who listened, and that transition places a responsibility on institutions like this House to ensure the testimony is preserved, taught and funded—properly and permanently. The second reason is that antisemitism, the oldest hatred, has not had the decency to remain in the past. It is present in our own country: in threats to Jewish schools and synagogues that require security at the door of every service, in conspiracy theories washing through social media, in the discourse of extremes on both ends of politics. Remembrance without vigilance is sentimentality. So today, let us do both. Let us honour the dead by name where we can, for each of the six million was a person and not a statistic. Let us thank the educators and the trusts who carry this work forward. And let us each leave this Chamber resolved that the words "never again" will be, in our time and on our watch, not an aspiration but a commitment.

Let us be clear about what sits behind these numbers, because they can sound like dry accountancy. Child maintenance is not a private matter between separated adults; it is money for children—for school shoes, for food, for heating the room a child does his homework in. The evidence is unambiguous that maintenance payments lift a significant number of children in separated families out of poverty, and that when payments fail, it is overwhelmingly children in the poorest households who bear the loss. And the enforcement system that should stand behind these obligations has become, for too many paying parents minded to avoid them, a paper tiger. The Select Committee and the NAO have both documented the pattern: collection charges that penalise the very families forced into the collect-and-pay system by non-compliance; enforcement powers—deduction orders, passport and licence removal, liability orders—used rarely and slowly; and self-employed non-resident parents able to minimise their declared income in ways that the service seems chronically unable to challenge. The measure of this system is not the sums assessed but the money that actually reaches children—and by that measure, we are failing them.

Communications. The EPA compiles the inventory in accordance with international reporting obligations, and its provisional figures for 2020 will be published in the normal cycle. What I can offer the Deputy at this stage is the broad picture as my Department understands it. The nature of agricultural emissions makes them quite different from those of transport or industry in how they responded to the pandemic. Transport emissions fell sharply during the restrictions because journeys simply stopped; agricultural activity, by contrast, continued largely unchanged, because animals must be fed, milked and cared for regardless of public health measures, and food production was rightly designated an essential activity throughout. Herd numbers, fertiliser use and the other principal drivers of agricultural emissions are influenced by market conditions, weather and policy far more than by the pandemic itself, and any pandemic effect in the 2020 inventory is therefore expected to be modest relative to other sectors. If anything, some patterns—strong dairy output responding to resilient international demand, for instance—operated in the opposite direction to the economy-wide decline. I would make the wider point that this underlines why our approach to agricultural emissions cannot rely on temporary disruptions but must rest on structural change, and that work is under way: the measures set out in the climate action plan for the sector, including improved breeding indices, protected urea, reduced chemical nitrogen use, and support for diversification into organics, forestry and tillage. These are the levers that will deliver a durable reduction trajectory consistent with the sectoral ceilings, while sustaining the family farm income on which rural Ireland depends. I have been consistent that I will not ask farmers to do this without support, and the reformed CAP strategic plan and national schemes are being aligned to reward climate action on the ground. When the EPA publishes the final 2020 inventory, my Department will of course study it closely, and I will arrange for the analysis to be shared with the Deputy and with the committee.

It is easy to forget, at this distance, what he gave up. A promising naval career—by every account of his contemporaries, a brilliant one, with first sea lord spoken of as a realistic destination—set aside in his early thirties, so that he could walk two paces behind for the rest of his long life. For a man of his restless energy and undoubted abilities, that renunciation cannot have been easy, and he was too honest a character ever to pretend otherwise. Consider the record: the hundreds of organisations he served, not as a name on notepaper but as an active, questioning, frequently demanding patron; the Duke of Edinburgh's Award, which has shaped the confidence and character of millions of young people in this country and around the world, and which may prove the most durable monument any public figure of his era leaves behind; his early and unfashionable championing of conservation and of industry, decades before either was popular. And through it all, the quality my constituents mention most when they speak of him: he was unmistakably himself. In an age of managed images, his directness—sometimes to the point of hazard—was a kind of honesty the public recognised and trusted. The grief felt across the country is not manufactured, and it is not really about ceremony at all. It is about a man who made a promise at Westminster Abbey in 1947 and kept it, without complaint and without holiday, for the better part of a century. This House honours him best by remembering that such service is possible, and by being unashamed to call it what it was: duty, fulfilled.

If they do not dispute them, the House is entitled to have that confirmed before, not after, the provisions take effect. The objection we will hear is that such reviews are unnecessary because the Treasury already publishes distributional analysis alongside fiscal events. does not speak in our name. Wales knows something about what it means to be received. Ask the Basque children who came to Caernarfonshire fleeing Franco's bombs. Ask the Belgian refugees welcomed into Welsh chapels and homes in the first war, or the Kindertransport children who found safety in our valleys. Ask the Ugandan Asians, the Vietnamese, the Syrians resettled in recent years in towns across Wales, where communities that have little themselves organised collections, taught English in church halls and stood at railway stations with signs of welcome. That is our tradition—the tradition of a nation of sanctuary, which the Senedd has embraced not as a slogan but as a programme—and this Bill sets its face against every part of it. Consider what the legislation actually does. It criminalises the act of arrival itself, punishing people not for what they have done but for the route they were forced to take—as though a person fleeing persecution can queue at an embassy that will not see them, for a safe route that does not exist. For the overwhelming majority of those crossing the Channel there is no visa, no scheme, no orderly queue; the safe routes Ministers invoke are, for most nationalities, a rhetorical device. It creates a two-tier system of protection that the UNHCR—the guardian of the very convention this country helped to draft in the shadow of the Holocaust—has said plainly is incompatible with our obligations. And the provisions on offshore processing borrow from a model whose documented results are despair, self-harm and enormous cost. None of this will stop the smugglers; the evidence is that deterrence of the desperate does not deter, it only drives people into more dangerous hands and more dangerous waters. So Wales says clearly: not in our name. I will vote against this Bill tonight, and I urge Members of every party and every nation of these islands to search their consciences and do the same.

But I say gently to the House: the referendum result was an instruction to leave the European Union; it was not an instruction to leave it in the most economically damaging way available, nor a prohibition on common sense. A 52-48 result is a mandate for departure with moderation—that is what those numbers mean in any democracy on earth. And the arithmetic of this House reflects the arithmetic of the country: there is no majority here for the hardest version of Brexit, and no majority for stopping it altogether. Those are facts, and facts are not betrayals. So the choice before us is not between purity and surrender; it is between compromise and paralysis. Paralysis has consequences—for investment that is already draining away, for the patience of the public, and for faith in this institution itself, which diminishes with every night of televised deadlock. I will vote for a compromise that delivers an orderly departure with a close economic relationship, and I will defend that vote to the 52% and the 48% alike, because in the end I was sent here to exercise judgment on behalf of both.

When Parliament passes legislation with terms this elastic, what we are really doing is delegating the hard decisions to officials, to regulators and ultimately to the courts, and every one of those decision-makers will fill the grey space differently. Consider what that means in practice for the people who must live under this law. A small operator trying to comply in good faith reads the bill and cannot determine, with any confidence, whether their ordinary activities fall inside or outside its scope. Their legal advice will be cautious, as legal advice always is, so they will over-comply—withdrawing services, restricting content, abandoning lines of business—not because Parliament decided those activities were harmful, but because Parliament declined to say whether they were. Meanwhile, the large incumbents, with their compliance departments and their litigation budgets, will test every ambiguity, secure in the knowledge that they can afford the fight. Vague law is regressive law: it burdens most heavily those least equipped to interpret it. And there is a deeper problem still, which goes to the role of this chamber. When we pass a bill whose key terms are undefined, we allow ourselves to vote for an aspiration while avoiding accountability for its application. Members can assure constituents the bill means one thing, the department can administer it as another, and when the results disappoint, everyone can say that was never the intent. That is not lawmaking; it is the outsourcing of lawmaking with extra steps. So my ask is straightforward, and it is one the government could accept without abandoning any of its stated objectives: define the operative terms in the bill itself; where discretion is genuinely necessary, structure it with criteria on the face of the legislation; and provide that the guidance which will inevitably follow comes back before Parliament for scrutiny. If the government knows what it means by this bill, it should have no difficulty writing it down. If it does not know, this House should not be voting for it.

Because that is what this motion is about, at its core: dignity, and whether we believe every person in this country is entitled to it, or only those fortunate enough to afford it. The bar of dignity in Canada today is set far too low, and I want to give the House some honest measurements. Dignity means being able to eat. Yet food bank usage has hit record highs, and the fastest-growing group of clients is people with jobs—working Canadians whose paycheques run out before the month does. Dignity means a roof over your head. Yet in every city and increasingly in every small town, encampments have become a permanent feature, rents have doubled in a decade, and a generation has quietly given up on the idea of ever owning a home. Dignity means being able to get sick without being ruined. Yet millions of Canadians cannot afford the dental care that keeps infection out of their bloodstream or the prescription drugs their doctors tell them they need; they are cutting pills in half at kitchen tables in every riding represented in this chamber, including those of members who will vote against this motion. And dignity means aging without fear, yet seniors who built this country are choosing between heat and groceries. Now, the response we always hear from the government benches is a recitation of programs and dollar figures, delivered as though the problem were that Canadians have failed to notice how well things are going. But people do not experience press releases; they experience prices. They experience the eighth ring of a phone at a clinic that is not taking patients. They experience the math of a paycheque that does not stretch. What this motion proposes is simple: that we measure our economy by whether ordinary people can live decent, secure lives—and that where the market fails to deliver that, as it plainly is failing, this Parliament acts: on dental care, on pharmacare, on housing, on the excess profits being taken at the very moment Canadians can least afford them.

The plants in question contain genetic changes of a kind that could have arisen through traditional breeding or through natural processes—no foreign genetic material is introduced. What the new techniques change is not the nature of the outcome but the speed and precision with which it can be reached. Traditional breeding shuffles thousands of genes over many generations in the hope of capturing a desired trait alongside who knows what else; precision breeding makes the specific change and only that change, with the result fully characterised. To regulate the faster, more precise route more severely than the slower, blunter one is not precaution; it is a category error, and it is a category error with real costs. Let me set out what those costs are. Our researchers—and this country is genuinely world-leading in plant science—have been unable to translate their work into varieties that farmers can grow, because the previous regime imposed processes so lengthy and expensive that only the largest multinational companies could afford them. The irony should not be lost on the House: a regime justified by suspicion of big business entrenched the market position of precisely those businesses, while pricing out public institutes and start-ups. Meanwhile the potential gains sit waiting: crops resistant to the diseases that currently demand repeated spraying, varieties that need less nitrogen fertiliser, plants resilient to the droughts and extremes that our own climate projections tell us are coming. Every year of delay is a year of higher pesticide use and lost resilience. I want to be equally clear about what the Bill does not do: it does not weaken the regulation of genuine transgenic organisms, which remain fully within the existing GMO framework, and it establishes a proportionate notification and assessment system, with food safety oversight, for precision-bred products. This is regulation following the science—precisely what Members on all sides say they want, and I commend it to the House.

Friend said earlier, a negotiation of this magnitude cannot be treated as the private property of the Executive, to be conducted in secret and revealed to Parliament only when the ink is dry and the choice has been reduced to take it or leave it. That is the constitutional question wrapped inside the economic one, and I want to address both. On the economics, the House should be under no illusion about what is at stake for constituencies like mine. The manufacturers who anchor our local economy operate just-in-time supply chains in which components cross borders multiple times before a finished product ships; even modest friction—an hour's delay, a customs declaration, a divergent standard—compounds across those crossings into costs that make plants uncompetitive against their sister sites inside the single market. Boardrooms deciding where the next production line goes do not shout about it; they simply allocate the investment elsewhere, and we discover the decision years later in jobs that were never created. The services firms, the universities, the farmers—each faces its own version of the same exposure. Against risks of that scale, the notion that Parliament should be a spectator is constitutionally absurd. We are told that scrutiny would tie the Government's hands—but every serious trading partner we face manages to combine democratic oversight with effective negotiation. Mandates are debated openly; legislatures are briefed in confidence; final texts receive genuine ratification votes. Only here is it suggested that democracy ends at the water's edge. So I support the motion before us, which asks for nothing more radical than this: that the Government publish their negotiating objectives in meaningful detail, provide for regular reporting to this House at each phase, and guarantee that the final agreement comes to Parliament with sufficient time for real scrutiny and a meaningful vote—not a revolver-on-the-table choice between the text and the abyss. Our constituents will live with the consequences for a generation. Their representatives are entitled to shape them.

That is the real cost, and it will outlast every one of us in this Chamber. The way to begin repairing it is not complicated: full accountability for those responsible, starting at the top, and an end to the insulting pretence that nothing of consequence occurred.

And if the mandate's public health rationale—that it protects others—no longer holds, then we are left compelling medical treatment for a benefit that accrues chiefly to the person compelled, which is a very different and much weaker justification for coercion in a free society. But having stated my agreement, let me be equally clear about where I part company with some of the rhetoric surrounding this debate. Questioning a mandate is not the same as questioning the vaccines. The evidence that vaccination dramatically reduces hospitalisation and death remains overwhelming, and I say to every constituent who asks me: I am vaccinated, my family is vaccinated, and I would encourage you without hesitation to be vaccinated too. The tragedy of the mandate policy is precisely that it has entangled a sound medical intervention with an unsound instrument of compulsion, allowing opponents of the former to cloak themselves in legitimate objections to the latter. Coercion has costs that do not appear in the modelling: it hardens hesitancy into resistance, it converts a health decision into an identity, and it hands a recruiting tool to those who traffic in genuine misinformation. Persuasion is slower, but its gains are durable; coercion's gains evaporate the moment enforcement does, leaving distrust behind as a residue. There is also the workforce question, which is stark in its simplicity: we are proposing to dismiss experienced staff from sectors that are desperately short of them, at the very moment of maximum strain. Whatever the marginal transmission benefit of mandating this workforce, it must be weighed against the certain harm of losing them, and I have yet to see the Government produce that analysis. So my position is this: promote vaccination relentlessly, make access effortless, answer hesitancy with patience and evidence—and reserve compulsion for circumstances where the case is overwhelming and current. That case has not been made, and the mandate should accordingly be suspended and reviewed.

But I want to step back from the argument about quantum, important as it is, because the deeper problem with local welfare provision is not only how much is allocated but whether anyone can find it, access it, or even discover that it exists. When the discretionary social fund was abolished and responsibility passed to local authorities without ring-fencing, we conducted, in effect, a natural experiment, and the results are now in. Some authorities have built genuinely effective schemes—cash grants, furniture and white goods provision, integrated with advice services. Others have reduced provision to vouchers with restrictive conditions. A significant number have closed their schemes entirely or run them so quietly that take-up is negligible, and the money, unprotected, has been absorbed into budgets hollowed out by a decade of cuts. The postcode lottery is not a rhetorical flourish; it is the literal description of the system. A family fleeing domestic violence, or a person leaving care or prison with nothing, will find a functioning safety net in one borough and a dead end in the neighbouring one, though their needs and their citizenship are identical. And the demand these schemes exist to meet has not diminished—every food bank, every advice centre, every Member's caseworker will testify that destitution-level crisis is more common, not less, than when the social fund was abolished. Crisis support is the cheapest intervention in the entire welfare landscape: a cooker, a deposit, a fortnight's food can be the difference between a household stabilising and a spiral into homelessness, care proceedings and costs a hundred times greater. So I put three propositions to the Minister. First, restore a ring fence, so that money voted for crisis support reaches crisis support. Second, set minimum national standards for eligibility and access, while leaving delivery local. Third, require publication of spending and take-up data, because what is unmeasured in this field has proven, time and again, to be what quietly disappears.

That is the distinction I want to draw out, because in the understandable rush to respond to the crisis there is a real danger that scarce public capital is allocated by the loudness of the lobby rather than the quality of the investment. The second is direction: if public money is to shape the economy that emerges from this crisis, let it shape the economy we actually need—the retrofitting industry that our climate obligations demand, the offshore wind supply chain we are perpetually about to develop, the digital infrastructure of regional towns, the water and housing systems whose deficits this crisis has exposed. Every one of those creates employment at least as effectively as the sectors demanding rescue, and creates it where it is needed. I am not arguing against supporting viable firms through a temporary shock—that is precisely what these instruments exist for. But viability must be tested honestly. Where a business model was failing before the pandemic, public money will not save it; it will only delay the reckoning at the citizens' expense, and starve the new economy of the capital it needs to grow. Other small states—the Danes, the Finns—have shown how state investment can be both disciplined and transformative. So I ask the Minister for a clear statement of the criteria that will govern these funds, the conditions that will attach to them—on employment, on emissions, on tax residence—and the mechanism by which the Oireachtas will scrutinise where the money actually goes.

That asymmetry, they say, tells them what society believes their lives are worth—and we must prove them wrong not with assurances but with the design of the law itself. So for me, the tests are these. Eligibility must be tightly drawn and clinically verified, with capacity assessed by professionals independent of one another. The request must originate with the person—never suggested, never prompted—and be tested for coercion, subtle as well as overt, with real investigative capacity behind that test. There must be genuine choice, which means palliative care funded and available to every person in every region, because a right to die chosen for want of decent care is no choice at all. If those safeguards hold, dignity is served at both ends. If they cannot be made to hold, we should not proceed.

The code exists, it has been published, and the question raised by the Deputy is the right one: is it actually working, or has it become one of those instruments that satisfies the letter of the Act while the substance carries on unaffected? Let me give the House my honest assessment. The Regulation of Lobbying Act was genuinely pioneering when it was enacted—the register is public, searchable and, by international standards, unusually comprehensive, and the three-times-yearly returns have thrown real light on who is seeking to influence whom about what. That should be acknowledged. But the transparency code for public bodies is the weakest link in the framework, for three reasons. First, awareness: the evidence from the Standards in Public Office Commission's own reports is that knowledge of the code among the relevant bodies—advisory groups, task forces, review panels—is patchy, and application is inconsistent. A code that designated officials have not read protects nobody. Second, enforcement: the code carries no meaningful sanction for non-observance. Where a public body simply fails to publish minutes of its engagement or the membership of its advisory structures, nothing follows. Third, scope: the ingenuity of those who wish to influence policy has moved on—informal channels, secondments, research bodies and representative associations that hover at the edges of the Act's definitions—while the code has stood still. So the review now under way must do more than tidy the drafting. I want to see the code given practical teeth: mandatory training for designated public officials; publication requirements with deadlines and a compliance report laid annually before the Oireachtas; and the extension of the framework to close the gaps that a decade of operation has revealed. Transparency is not an event, it is a discipline, and disciplines require maintenance. I will bring proposals to Government on foot of the review, and I welcome the scrutiny of this House in that work.

That settlement has served this country for centuries, through crises considerably graver than the present one, and the reason it works is that each part knows its role. The Government governs; Parliament holds it to account; neither steals the other's function. The proposals we have debated today would upset that balance, not in favour of the people, as their advocates claim, but in favour of whichever faction can best exploit the machinery of the Order Paper on a given afternoon. Let me address directly the argument that exceptional times justify exceptional procedure. Every generation believes its emergency is unique, and every erosion of constitutional practice is first proposed as a one-off. But Standing Orders are not the property of any Parliament or any cause; they are the accumulated wisdom of centuries about how a chamber of rivals can transact business without descending into procedural warfare, and they will be needed long after the present controversy is forgotten—by majorities and minorities not yet imagined, on questions not yet conceived. A precedent set today in the service of an outcome I might even favour will be available tomorrow in the service of outcomes I dread, wielded by hands I do not know. That is the test any constitutional change must pass: not "does it help my side now?" but "would I accept it used against me?" And the honest answer, for the proposals before us, is no. If the Government of the day loses the confidence of this House, the constitution provides the remedy, and it is a clean one. What it does not provide, and should not, is a mechanism by which the House becomes the Executive for an afternoon at a time, accountable to no one, before handing back the keys. The settlement works. We tamper with it in the heat of a single controversy at our lasting peril, and I urge the House to stand by it.

First, on supply: what precisely are the confirmed delivery schedules from each manufacturer for the coming month—not the contracted totals for the year, which tell us nothing, but the actual doses arriving in the actual weeks ahead? If there is a shortfall, tell the country plainly, because people can handle honesty far better than they handle moving targets. Second, on administration: when supply does arrive, is every channel being used to put it into arms within days rather than weeks—GPs, pharmacies, mass vaccination centres, evening and weekend capacity? Other countries are vaccinating around the clock; there is no reason we cannot. Third, on prioritisation: the sequencing of cohorts must follow the medical evidence on risk, and where there are anomalies—carers, people with underlying conditions falling between categories—they need resolution now, not after the cohort has passed. We all want the roll-out to win—the Taoiseach and I agree on that much. But wanting is not a strategy, and the variant is not waiting.

First, through our media freedom campaign and the coalition of governments we co-founded, we raise these cases publicly and privately at the highest levels—and I can tell my hon. Second, we fund the legal defence of journalists under attack through the Media Legal Defence funds our programmes support; the High Level Panel of Legal Experts, which Amal Clooney chairs, exists precisely to put the world's best legal minds at the service of persecuted reporters. Third, we have created a sanctions regime that allows us to target individuals responsible for serious human rights violations, and I do not exclude its use in cases involving the persecution of journalists. It means that major projects proceed when, and only when, the Crown has discharged its duties—to the environment, and to the constitutionally protected rights of indigenous peoples. It does not mean that any single objection, however sincerely held, carries a veto over the national interest. The court did not say this project could never be built; it said the work had to be done right, and we have done it right. Bill does not alter who can perform abortions, where they can be performed, or the requirement for two doctors' involvement in the later stages; what it removes is the threat of prosecution—of the woman herself, and of the clinicians acting in good faith—that hangs over what is, and should be treated as, a healthcare decision. I ask the House to consider what the current law actually is. The foundation remains a Victorian statute, passed decades before women could vote, which makes abortion a criminal offence carrying a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, with the modern framework operating only as a set of exemptions to that criminal prohibition. That architecture has consequences. Women who end pregnancies outside the strict terms of the exemptions—frightened women, sometimes very young, sometimes victims of abuse, sometimes women who bought pills online because they could not navigate the system—have faced police investigation and prosecution in this country, in recent years, under that Victorian Act. Clinicians practise under a criminal shadow that shapes their decisions in ways no other field of medicine experiences, and which the professional bodies tell us deters doctors from entering this area of practice at all. Decriminalisation is not a novel experiment; it is the settled position of the royal colleges and the approach adopted, without the predicted harms, in other jurisdictions of these islands and beyond. Where it has been implemented, abortion has not become more common, nor later; it has simply been governed, as all healthcare is governed, by regulation, professional standards and the ordinary criminal law that protects everyone from malpractice and coercion—every one of which my Bill preserves. What changes is that a woman in crisis is met as a patient, not a suspect. That is the whole of it. Suspicionless stop and search is among the most intrusive powers the state possesses short of arrest. Used with individual suspicion, search powers are a normal tool of policing; stripped of that requirement, they become something categorically different—a power to stop any person, in a designated area, who has done nothing whatsoever to attract attention. We know from the long history of such powers where that leads, because we have been here before: the evidence from previous suspicionless regimes showed vanishingly small arrest rates, gross racial disproportionality in their use, and lasting damage to the confidence of the very communities whose cooperation policing depends upon—which is why Parliament and the courts curtailed them. Now they return, attached not to terrorism but to protest, in the political heart of the capital. And consider what Parliament Square is. It is the place where the suffragettes chained themselves, where causes from every tradition represented in this House have assembled to be heard. To subject that ground, of all ground, to a regime in which a person may be stopped and searched on no suspicion at all—a journalist, a protester, a member of the public, or indeed, as my example suggests, those who work in this building—is to invert the relationship between citizen and state that the square exists to symbolise. The Minister will say the powers will be used proportionately. But we do not legislate for the ministers and officers we hope for; we legislate for the worst hands the powers may fall into. I ask the House to support the amendments removing these provisions, and to remember that the liberties most easily surrendered in the name of order are the ones we spend generations trying to recover.

It is right that this House pauses on the human beings before it turns to the mechanics, because behind every number in the statement is a name, a family, a street that will never be quite the same. Our first duty is to them, and I welcome the tone the right hon. Lady has struck. But compassion, to mean anything, must be followed by action in three respects, and I want to put each to her directly. The first is the immediate relief effort: the affected families need shelter, financial assistance and practical support now—not after assessments and application processes have wound their course. Emergency payments should be flowing within days, and I would be grateful for her assurance that the resources on the ground match the scale of the need, and that anyone falling through gaps between agencies has a single point of contact to turn to. The second is the investigation. The survivors and the bereaved are entitled to the truth—the full truth, arrived at independently, however uncomfortable it proves for any institution, public or private. The questions are already forming: what warnings were given, what inspections were carried out, what was known and by whom. I ask her to commit that the investigation will have the independence, the powers and the resources to answer them, and that the families will be at its centre, kept informed at every stage rather than reading developments in the press. The third is prevention. When the facts are established, if they reveal—as such tragedies too often do—that warnings went unheeded or standards were allowed to slip, then the changes must actually be made, promptly and in full. The gravest disrespect we could show the dead is a report that joins its predecessors on a shelf. Grief will be with the families for the rest of their lives; our obligations to them should last at least as long as that. If the right hon. Lady proceeds in that spirit, she will have our support at every step.
